definition: Moderation and self-control, especially in eating, spending, or other pleasures.
example: Grandpa credited his long life to temperance: small meals, early nights, and daily walks.
nuance: Temperance is restraint in one's appetites; don't confuse it with temperament, which is a person's natural disposition.
prompt: A teenager receives a generous sum of birthday money and must decide how to spend it.
options: Showing temperance, he spent a little on a novel and saved the rest for summer.
The temperance in the store was so high that he took off his jacket.
In a fit of temperance, he spent every dollar within an hour on snacks.
His temperance flared when the cashier gave him the wrong change, and he shouted at her.
reasons: Treating himself modestly and holding back the rest is exactly this kind of restraint.
This confuses the word with temperature; it describes self-control, not heat.
Blowing all the money at once is excess, the reverse of moderation.
This mixes the word up with temper; it means calm restraint, not an angry outburst.

practice.prompt: A family on vacation visits an all-you-can-eat buffet.
options: Mia's temperance led her to pile four plates high and keep eating until she felt sick.
Mia has a high temperance for spicy food, so the hot curry didn't bother her.
With great temperance, the waiter refused to refill anyone's water glass.
Practicing temperance, Mia took one small plate and stopped once she was full.
reasons: Eating until sick is overindulgence, the opposite of self-restraint.
This confuses the word with tolerance; it is about restraint, not handling spice.
The word means limiting your own appetites, not denying things to other people.
Choosing a reasonable amount despite unlimited food shows moderation.
